Shapes of Constant Width

AreaLimitsAlgebra
Game: A rounded triangle turns inside a square and never stops touching all four sides; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Watch it turn. Click the picture (or press View) to change what you see: the triangle turning, the square turning round it, or the ground the triangle covers.

Click the picture or press Enter for the next view. Space pauses; the arrow keys turn it.

Look for the math

You cannot drill a square hole with a round drill, but with a rounded triangle you can come very close, because that triangle has the same width in every direction.

Width and the Reuleaux triangle

Squeeze a shape between two parallel lines, as tight as it will go: the distance between them is its width in that direction. A circle has the same width everywhere. So does the Reuleaux triangle: start with an equilateral triangle of side s and bulge each side into an arc of radius s centred at the opposite vertex. The logic test measured its width in every direction (one degree apart) at every angle of the applet and always found exactly s.

Inside a square

Because the width is s both across and up, the shape always fits snugly in a square of side s, touching all four sides as it turns. The applet finds that square without calculus: where an arc (not a corner) is the extreme side, the opposite side is a corner, s away. As it turns, the triangle covers almost the whole square, leaving only the four corners nearly untouched: the area covered is 2√3 + π/6 − 3 ≈ 0.98770 of a square of side 1, found here by counting grid points and agreeing to three decimal places.

Area and perimeter

Its area is (π − √3)/2 · s² ≈ 0.7048 s², less than the circle of the same width, π/4 · s² ≈ 0.7854 s². Its perimeter is three arcs of 60°, that is π s: the same formula as a circle of diameter s, which is Barbier’s theorem: the perimeter of every shape of constant width s is π s. Its three corners are 120° angles. And if a triangle of side 50 has its sides extended 10 beyond each corner and arcs added in the same way, the width is 50 + 2 · 10 = 70.

The page says the applet has three modes; the original cycles through four settings with each click. This port keeps the three described on the page.

Pause, then turn it with the arrow keys and watch which side of the square is touched by a corner and which by an arc. Then switch to the trace view.
